flashcards.q: 1a Variable vs constant in C# (3)
flashcards.a: Variable value can change (int age=20;). Constant is fixed at compile time (const double PI=3.14;).

flashcards.q: 1b Three rules for identifiers (3)
flashcards.a: Start with a letter or underscore; no spaces or special symbols; cannot be a keyword; case-sensitive.

flashcards.q: 1c Expression with arithmetic, relational, logical operators (6)
flashcards.a: if ((a + b) * 2 > 20 && a != b) { ... }  Arithmetic: + and *; relational: > and !=; logical: &&.

flashcards.q: 1d Define an event in Windows Forms with example (4)
flashcards.a: An action that happens to a control and triggers code, e.g. a Button Click or TextBox TextChanged.

flashcards.q: 1e How a click event handler works (5)
flashcards.a: private void btnOk_Click(object sender, EventArgs e){ lblMsg.Text="Hello"; }  The handler is subscribed to the Click event; when clicked, the runtime calls it.

flashcards.q: 1f Declare and print student's name, age, grade (3)
flashcards.a: string name="Ann"; int age=20; char grade='A'; Console.WriteLine(name+" "+age+" "+grade);

flashcards.q: 1g Four reasons event-driven programming matters + example (5)
flashcards.a: Responsive UI; user controls the flow; efficient (code runs only on events); modular handlers. Example: a POS app that updates totals when a button is clicked.

flashcards.q: 2a Three examples of properties of controls (6)
flashcards.a: Text (caption), BackColor (colour), Enabled (can interact); also Name, Size, Visible.

flashcards.q: 2b btnSubmit shows 'Submitted successfully!' (6)
flashcards.a: private void btnSubmit_Click(object sender, EventArgs e){ MessageBox.Show("Submitted successfully!"); }

flashcards.q: 2c Design-time vs run-time properties (4)
flashcards.a: Design-time: set in the Properties window (button1.Text='Save'). Run-time: set in code (button1.Text='Saving...').

flashcards.q: 2d Four reasons to manage property values properly (4)
flashcards.a: Consistent appearance; prevent invalid input (Enabled/ReadOnly); better usability and accessibility; easier maintenance.

flashcards.q: 3a Purpose of project documentation (4)
flashcards.a: Records requirements, design and usage; helps maintenance and handover; communication; supports testing and training.

flashcards.q: 3b Modal vs modeless dialog forms (4)
flashcards.a: Modal: must be closed before using the parent (ShowDialog()). Modeless: user can switch freely (Show()).

flashcards.q: 3c Three purposes of a dialog box in student registration (6)
flashcards.a: Confirm actions (delete); show messages/errors; collect extra input (login, choose course); open/save files.

flashcards.q: 3d Implement a login dialog in a SIMS (6)
flashcards.a: Create frmLogin with username, password (UseSystemPasswordChar), Login button; on click validate against database; if valid, DialogResult.OK and open the main form; limit attempts.

flashcards.q: 4a User requirements and four reasons they're critical (6)
flashcards.a: Needs and expectations from users. Critical: guide design, avoid rework, set scope, basis for testing, user satisfaction.

flashcards.q: 4b Four SIMS requirements (4)
flashcards.a: Register students; record grades; view/search records; generate reports; user login.

flashcards.q: 4c Translating requirements into UI design (6)
flashcards.a: Analyse requirements → identify inputs/outputs → choose controls → sketch forms → map actions to events → test with users.

flashcards.q: 4d Three SIMS requirements mapped to Windows Form features (4)
flashcards.a: Enter student details → TextBoxes; select course → ComboBox; save record → Button with Click handler.

flashcards.q: 5a Form in Windows Forms vs console window (4)
flashcards.a: A form is a graphical window holding controls and responding to events; a console is text-only, sequential input/output.

flashcards.q: 5b Steps to create a Windows Form in Visual Studio (6)
flashcards.a: File > New > Project; choose Windows Forms App; name and create; Form1 appears in designer; add controls from Toolbox; set properties; double-click to write handlers; run.

flashcards.q: 5c Three common controls and use cases (6)
flashcards.a: TextBox: user text input. Button: triggers actions. Label: displays text/instructions. (Also ComboBox, CheckBox.)

flashcards.q: 5d Three factors why form design matters (4)
flashcards.a: Usability and ease of learning; efficiency and fewer errors; consistent professional look.
